meta.description: No — Maya Angelou almost certainly didn't coin this. The line traces to a saying credited to LDS leader Carl W. Buehner in 1971, decades before it reached Angelou.

answer.label: Not Maya Angelou — traces to Carl W. Buehner
answer.authorDates: 1898–1974 · Latter-day Saint leader & Salt Lake City businessman
answer.sourceLine: The earliest documented form is credited to Carl W. Buehner in Richard Evans’ Quote Book (1971): “They may forget what you said — but they will never forget how you made them feel.” The Maya Angelou attribution doesn’t surface until 2003, and no interview or book of hers has been found using these words. The now-familiar wording — which adds “people will forget what you did” — is a later, expanded paraphrase of Buehner’s line.

source.excerpt: They may forget what you said — but they will never forget how you made them feel.
trail: 1971: Richard Evans’ Quote Book prints “They may forget what you said — but they will never forget how you made them feel,” credited to Carl W. Buehner, per Quote Investigator.
2003: The saying first appears attributed to Maya Angelou — in an expanded form adding “people will forget what you did” — which QI judges “unsupported and inaccurate.”
Today: Wikiquote files it under Misattributed, noting it is “a very close paraphrase” of the Buehner line.
source.excerptNote: The form credited to Carl W. Buehner in Richard Evans’ Quote Book (1971). The popular “People will forget what you said, people will forget what you did…” version is a later expansion attributed to Maya Angelou.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording — with “people will forget what you did” — is an anonymous paraphrase with no identified author or source, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. The nearest documented ancestor, the Buehner-credited line in Richard Evans’ Quote Book (1971), would itself be in copyright as a 1971 publication; nothing here is public domain.

author.name: Carl W. Buehner
author.heading: Who was Carl W. Buehner?
author.metaLine: 1898–1974 · Latter-day Saint leader & Salt Lake City businessman
author.bio: Carl William Buehner (1898–1974) was a German-born American businessman and leader in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, serving as second counselor in the Presiding Bishopric from 1952 to 1961. A frequent speaker, he is the earliest documented figure credited with the saying “They may forget what you said — but they will never forget how you made them feel,” recorded in Richard Evans’ Quote Book in 1971. The line later drifted, in expanded form, onto Maya Angelou.

misattribution.heading: How this became a “Maya Angelou” quote
misattribution.intro: It’s one of the internet’s most-shared “Maya Angelou” lines — but the paper trail points somewhere else entirely.

items.why: The version beginning “People will forget what you said, people will forget what you did…” is credited to Angelou from about 2003 onward, but Quote Investigator found no interview, speech, or book in which she uses it and calls the ascription “unsupported and inaccurate.”
Some collections credit a “Carol Buchner,” which QI concludes is a mistranscription of Carl W. Buehner’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented form credits Carl W. Buehner in 1971; the Angelou version is a later, expanded paraphrase.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Angelou
lead: Maya Angelou is one of the internet’s biggest “quote magnets”: warm, wise-sounding lines gravitate to her name because it lends instant authority. This saying about how people remember feelings fits her public voice so well that few readers pause to ask whether she ever actually said it.

The trail, though, runs through a 1971 Latter-day Saint quotation book, not through any of Angelou’s poems, memoirs, or interviews — and the wording most people share is a paraphrase that grew a whole extra clause along the way.
context.pull: A line so “Angelou” that no one checked whether it was hers.
